messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 32
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Tutor
- Trauma Type: Stalking
- Pcl5: 59

He is thirty-two years old, married for six years, and works as a private tutor—a job he once loved because it allowed him to help struggling students find their footing. He meets with clients in coffee shops, libraries, and occasionally at their homes. But for the past two years, his life has been shaped by something that happened long before those sessions.

It began during his second year of tutoring when a nineteen-year-old student, a young woman he was helping with college entrance exams, started sending him messages far beyond academic questions. At first they were harmless—compliments on his patience, questions about his weekend. Then came multiple texts a day, photographs of places he went, and voicemails at night. She began waiting outside the library where he tutored, sometimes holding a coffee she bought for him. He asked her to stop. She did not. His wife noticed his rising anxiety, and together they contacted the police. A restraining order was issued. The student’s behavior escalated—a brick through their living room window, a letter slipped under their door. The case went to court, and after several months she was sentenced to probation and ordered to stay away. He has not seen her since.

He wishes he could say that was the end. But the experience has rewired the way he moves through the world. Every tutoring session begins with a ritual: he scans the parking lot before entering a coffee shop, chooses a seat facing the door, and keeps his phone on the table face-up so he can see notifications. When a new client contacts him, he spends hours searching their name online, looking for any sign of instability. He turned down a high-paying student last month because her last name was similar to his stalker’s.

At home, he flinches at the sound of his phone buzzing. His wife touches his shoulder from behind and he jerks away. They used to talk openly about their day; now he spends evenings in silence, replaying the time she stood outside his car, the way she smiled when he begged her to leave. He has stopped going to the grocery store alone. He double-checks the locks on every door before bed, sometimes three times. If he sees a car that matches the make and model his stalker drove, his heart pounds and his palms sweat—even if it is a different color, even if she lives in another state now.

His tutoring work suffers in subtler ways. During sessions, his mind drifts. He hears a chair scrape behind him and forgets what he was explaining. A student asks a question and he answers with a curt, irritable tone that he regrets instantly. He has lost two clients who complained he seemed “distracted.” He no longer tutors in the evening because darkness makes him feel exposed. He tells himself this is reasonable caution, but he knows it has become something more. He tries to push the memories away, but they return without warning: the sound of her voice on his voicemail, the way his wife’s face looked the night of the broken window.

He feels guilt that he cannot simply “move on.” He feels shame that a grown man can be undone by a woman half his age. He has stopped talking about it with friends because he can see their confusion—*Didn’t that end years ago?*—and he knows they cannot understand why he still checks his rearview mirror on every drive, why he cannot sit with his back to a door, why the word *obsession* makes him freeze. He is a tutor, a husband, a man trying to keep his life in order, but the past keeps reaching through the present, and he does not know how to stop it.
